8.title: the greeting that is a wish
8.hook: the greeting that is a wish; s-l-m — salaam, Muslim, Islam
8.howItsDone: Muslims greet one another with "as-salamu alaykum" (peace be upon you) and answer "wa alaykum as-salam" (and upon you peace), often adding "and the mercy of God and His blessings." The greeting is also said to close each daily prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Eid, joy that comes back around. That was week one. Week two starts with the first word two Muslims say to each other. Day eight.

In a shop, at an airport gate, across a dinner table: two people meet, and before how are you, before the weather, one says as-salamu alaykum. The other answers straight back: wa alaykum as-salam. It happens so fast it sounds like hello. It isn't hello. Hello says I see you. This greeting hands the other person something. And the word at its center is hiding inside the name of the faith itself.
screen: `AS-SALAMU ALAYKUM.` → `IT SOUNDS LIKE HELLO.` → `IT'S A WISH.`

segments.voice: Salaam means peace. As-salamu alaykum: peace be upon you. A wish, given in the first second of meeting someone. Here's the part that surprises people. Arabic builds its words from roots, usually three letters. This one is s, l, m. Put different vowels around it and you get salaam: peace. You get Islam: the surrender, the making of peace with God. And you get Muslim: a person who does that. So every time two Muslims greet each other, they say a piece of the faith's own name. The Qur'an even gives the word to God: among God's names is As-Salam, Peace itself. And it sets a rule for answering: “When ye are greeted with a greeting, greet ye with a better than it or return it.” The minimum is to give the peace back. Better is to add to it: and upon you peace, and the mercy of God, and His blessings. The greeting grows as it goes around. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ ties it to love: you won't truly love one another, he told his companions, until you spread salaam among yourselves. Not a feeling first and then a greeting. The greeting first, and the love grows from it.
screen: `SALAAM — PEACE.` · `S-L-M: SALAAM, ISLAM, MUSLIM.` · `ANSWER WITH BETTER, OR THE SAME.` · `THE GREETING FIRST, THEN THE LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Bring to mind one person you'll see today. Breathe in, and on the way out send them the word, silently: salaam, peace upon you. Then someone harder to greet. The same word, the same breath. Stay with it.
Salaam. Peace: the greeting that's a gift, and the root inside Islam and Muslim. Eighth word.
Your line: peace, upon you. The Qur'an's rule for answering: with better, or at least the same. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A HOUSE BUILT ON FIVE.`

9.title: a house built on five
9.hook: not a checklist: a building, and the building is made of time
9.carry: five things that hold a life up
9.howItsDone: Muslims keep the five together: the shahada as the core of faith, the five daily prayers, zakat given yearly, the Ramadan fast, and the hajj once in a lifetime for those able. Shia Muslims keep the same practices and describe the faith as roots (beliefs) and branches (practices).

segments.voice: Yesterday: salaam. Your line was peace, upon you. Today, the whole shape of a Muslim life, in one sitting. Day nine.

The five pillars of Islam often get learned like a list for a test. Witness. Prayer. Giving. Fasting. Pilgrimage. Five boxes, done. Said that way, it sounds like a checklist. But the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ didn't describe them as a list. He described them as a building. And the building turns out to be made of time.
screen: `FIVE WORDS, FIVE BOXES?` → `NOT A CHECKLIST.` → `A BUILDING.`

segments.voice: Islam is built on five, a saying of the Prophet goes. Built, like a house; pillars are what keep the roof up. One: the shahada, the witness. There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. One sentence, said to become Muslim and said inside every prayer. Its clock is always. Two: salat, prayer, five times a day, at times that move with the sun. Its clock is the day. Three: zakat, giving a set share of savings to people in need, once a year. Four: sawm, the Ramadan fast you met on day six. Their clock is the year. Five: hajj, the pilgrimage to Mecca, once in a lifetime. Its clock is a life. Now look at the shape. Always. Every day. Every year. Once in a life. Circles inside circles. And the house fits the person living in it: the Qur'an lets the sick and the traveler make up missed fast days, and asks for the hajj only from those able to make the journey. Muslims also draw the house in more than one way. Sunni teaching usually names these five as the pillars. Shia teaching usually speaks of roots, the core beliefs, and branches, the practices: the witness lives in the roots, and prayer, fasting, giving and pilgrimage among the branches. Same house, drawn two ways.
screen: `ISLAM IS BUILT ON FIVE.` · `ALWAYS, DAILY, YEARLY, ONCE.` · `BUILT TO FIT THE PERSON.` · `ROOTS AND BRANCHES: DRAWN TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. The pillars are circles of time, so borrow the shape. Bring to mind something that holds up your day, and let it stay a moment. Then something that holds up your year. Then something you'd want to do once in your life. Nothing to do about any of them. Just see what's holding you up.
The five pillars. Witness, prayer, giving, fasting, pilgrimage: not five boxes but a house built on five. Ninth word.
Your line: five things that hold a life up. Always, daily, yearly, once. Day nine.

10.title: why five times
10.hook: why five times; standing, bowing, forehead to the ground
10.howItsDone: Muslims pray salat five times a day, facing Mecca, in a set sequence of standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting; they may pray at home, at work, at a mosque, or anywhere clean.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the five pillars, a house built on five. Today, the second pillar, up close. Day ten.
screen: `THE FIVE PILLARS — A HOUSE BUILT ON FIVE.` → `DAY 10.`

segments.voice: Ten past one on a weekday, in the stockroom behind a hardware store. One of the staff flattens a clean cardboard box on the floor, turns to face a particular direction, and stands very still. Then he bows, hands on his knees. Then he goes all the way down, forehead to the cardboard, between the paint cans and the delivery crates. A few minutes later he folds the box away and goes back to the register. Why five times a day? And why the whole body?
screen: `A STOCKROOM, JUST AFTER ONE.` → `FOREHEAD TO THE FLOOR.` → `WHY FIVE? WHY THE BODY?`

segments.voice: Salat. It's the second pillar, and it isn't quite what English means by prayer. Du'a is asking, in your own words, any time. Salat is a set shape, at set times, with set words. The Qur'an says: “Lo! worship preserveth from lewdness and iniquity.” The five times follow the sun. Fajr before sunrise. Dhuhr after midday. Asr in the afternoon. Maghrib just after sunset. Isha at night. Where does five come from? A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells it. On the Night Journey he was given fifty daily prayers. On the way back, Musa, Moses, asked what he'd been given, and said: your people can't manage that; go back and ask for less. He went back, again and again, until it was five. And God said: five, with the reward of fifty. Many pray them at five separate times; Shia practice also allows joining them into three sittings, and the prayers are still five. Now the body. Each prayer is made of units called rak'ahs, and each moves through the same shapes. Standing, and reciting al-Fatiha, the seven verses from day two. Bowing, back flat, hands on the knees. Standing again. Then sujud: forehead, nose, palms, knees and toes on the ground. Another saying tells that a person is never nearer to God than there. The part of you that thinks, set down where your feet were.
screen: `SALAT — A SET SHAPE, AT SET TIMES.` · `FIVE TIMES, FOLLOWING THE SUN.` · `FIFTY, THEN FIVE.` · `STANDING, BOWING, FOREHEAD DOWN.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand for a moment, then bow a little, hands on your knees, and notice how your breath changes in each shape. If you'd rather stay seated, lower your head toward your chest, slowly, and feel what the body says when it bows. Stay there, and let the body do the praying for once, without any words.
Salat. The prayer in its set shape: five times a day, standing, bowing, forehead to the ground. Tenth word.
Your line: the body prays too. And if you prayed for a while and then stopped, you're in plenty of company: many come back one prayer at a time. Day ten.

11.title: thank-you as a reflex
11.tomorrow: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
11.howItsDone: Muslims say alhamdulillah when asked how they are, after meals, after sneezing, and at good news and hard news alike; after the prayer many repeat it thirty-three times, counting on their fingers or prayer beads.

segments.voice: Yesterday: salat. Your line was the body prays too. Today, a word many Muslims say once the prayer is done, and all day long. Day eleven.

Ask a Muslim friend how they are, and there's a good chance the first word back isn't fine. It's alhamdulillah. Got the job? Alhamdulillah. Didn't get the job? Very often, also alhamdulillah. Someone sneezes: alhamdulillah. A grandmother, asked about her knees, which are terrible: alhamdulillah. It comes out so fast it sounds like a reflex. It is one, but a reflex people build on purpose, and the word says more than thanks.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU?` → `GOT THE JOB. DIDN'T GET THE JOB.` → `THE SAME WORD, EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Al-hamdu li-llah. Al: the. Hamd: praise. Li-llah: belongs to God. The praise belongs to God. Not quite thanks, God. Arabic has a separate word for thanks, shukr, and scholars draw a line between the two. Thanks answers something done for you. Praise answers who someone is. You can only give thanks for the good day; you can give praise on any day. That's why the word keeps turning up on the bad ones. The root of hamd, h-m-d, is in a name you know. Muhammad means the one who is praised, again and again. Ahmad, Mahmoud, Hamid: the same three letters. It's woven into the day. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says: when you sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, may God have mercy on you. After the prayer, many count it thirty-three times, on their fingers or on beads, among other short phrases. And another saying explains why it fits any kind of day. The believer's situation is a wonder, the Prophet said: when good comes, they're grateful, and that's good for them; when hardship comes, they're patient, and that's good for them too. Alhamdulillah is the two-second version. It doesn't pretend the bad day was good. It says the praise still belongs where it belonged this morning.
screen: `THE PRAISE BELONGS TO GOD.` · `PRAISE, NOT ONLY THANKS.` · `H-M-D — THE ROOT OF MUHAMMAD.` · `GOOD DAY OR HARD DAY, BOTH COUNT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one thing that went right today, and stay with it. Then one thing that didn't. Then hold both at once, the good one and the hard one, and notice they belong to the same day. If you want, let the word ride out on a breath: alhamdulillah.
Alhamdulillah. The praise belongs to God. Praise, not only thanks, so it fits every kind of day. Eleventh word.
Your line: praise, whatever the day did. It fits the good days and the hard ones. Day eleven.

screen: `DAY 11 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "PRAISE BE TO ALLAH, LORD OF THE WORLDS."`

12.title: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds"
12.hook: the lord who raises and tends every world, not just yours
12.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in Arabic in every unit of every prayer, and many say alhamdulillah, its opening word, many times a day. Rabb is also the word Muslims use in many personal prayers, often as Rabbi, my Lord, or Rabbana, our Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday: alhamdulillah, the praise belongs to God. Today it turns out to be the first word of a verse you say in every prayer. Day twelve.

On day two you heard al-Fatiha whole, all seven verses in one go. For the next five days it slows down: one verse at a time, inside words you may have said a thousand times. Verse two begins with yesterday's word. Praise be to God. Then it points that praise somewhere enormous. Not at your day. At every world there is.
screen: `AL-FATIHA, SLOWED DOWN.` → `VERSE TWO: ALHAMDULILLAH.` → `EVERY WORLD THERE IS.`

segments.voice: Verse two: “Praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.” In Arabic, al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin. The first half is yesterday's word. The new word is Rabb. English says Lord, which is right, but thin. Rabb is the one who owns and the one who looks after. Commentators explain it with the picture of raising something: bringing a child, or a seedling, along step by step until it's grown. So a rabb isn't a distant owner with paperwork. It's the one who feeds, shelters and brings you up. Then al-'alamin: the worlds. Not the world: the worlds, plural. Commentators have listed people, angels, animals, every kind of created thing. The ant colony under the sidewalk. The deep sea. The inside of a stranger's life on the train. All of it, the verse says, is being raised and tended by one Rabb. And remember the conversation from day two. At this verse, God answers: My servant has praised Me. The praise isn't said into empty air. It's heard, and answered.
screen: `ALHAMDULILLAH — ALL PRAISE.` · `RABB — THE ONE WHO RAISES.` · `AL-'ALAMIN — THE WORLDS, PLURAL.` · `MY SERVANT HAS PRAISED ME.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. First, your own world: one thing in it that's being looked after, even today. Stay with it. Then a world that isn't yours: a bird, a stranger, a field somewhere you'll never see. Then hold both at once. If you want, the Arabic can ride out on a breath: al-hamdu lillahi rabbi l-'alamin.
Rabb. Lord: the one who owns, raises and looks after, here the Lord of all the worlds. Twelfth word.
Your line: every world is tended. Yours, and every one you'll never see. Day twelve.

13.title: "The Beneficent, the Merciful"
13.hook: mercy, named twice, before the word judgment ever appears
13.howItsDone: Muslims say these two names in every unit of every prayer, twice over: in the bismillah and again in verse three. Ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim are also among the names of God Muslims call on in their own prayers, and children are given the names Abdur-Rahman and Abdur-Rahim, servant of the Merciful.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rabb, the one who raises and looks after every world. Your line was every world is tended. Day thirteen.

A mare stands in a field with her foal pressed close against her legs. She's about to shift her weight, and she stops, lifts one hoof, and holds it in the air, so she won't step on him. A saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ uses exactly that picture: the gentleness creatures show each other comes from one small share of a much greater mercy. Today's verse is two words long, and both of them are that mercy.
screen: `A MARE LIFTS HER HOOF.` → `ONE SHARE OF MERCY.` → `VERSE THREE: TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: Verse three: “The Beneficent, the Merciful.” Ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. If that sounds familiar, it should: they're the two names from verse one, the bismillah, said again. Both come from one root, r-h-m, and the noun is today's word: rahma, mercy. The same root makes rahim, the womb. In this language, mercy has the shape of the place where you were held before you were born. Why two names? One common explanation: ar-Rahman is mercy as wide as everything, reaching every creature. Ar-Rahim is mercy that stays, that keeps coming back to you in particular. And the mare? The same saying says God made mercy in a hundred parts and sent one part into the world. With that one part, creatures are gentle with each other. The other ninety-nine are kept back. Now look at where the verse sits. Praise, then mercy, then mercy again, and only after that, tomorrow, the word judgment. Another saying puts it plainly: when God created the world, He wrote that His mercy outstrips His anger. And in the conversation from day two, God answers this verse too: My servant has extolled Me.
screen: `THE TWO NAMES FROM VERSE ONE.` · `R-H-M — THE ROOT OF WOMB.` · `WIDE MERCY, MERCY THAT STAYS.` · `MERCY OUTSTRIPS ANGER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. First, the wide mercy: something good that reaches everyone, sunlight, rain, the air in this breath. Stay with it. Then the mercy that stays: someone who kept coming back for you, even when you didn't make it easy. Let their face come. If you pray, you can hold the two names: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. If you don't, hold the two pictures.
Rahma. Mercy, from the root of the womb, named twice in a row: ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim. Thirteenth word.
Your line: mercy twice before anything else. That's the order the prayer keeps. Day thirteen.

14.title: "Owner of the Day of Judgment"
14.hook: a day when every account is settled, held by the one just named merciful
14.carry: the account is in kind hands
14.tomorrow: "Thee (alone) we worship; Thee (alone) we ask for help"
14.howItsDone: Muslims say this verse in every unit of every prayer. Belief in the Last Day is one of the articles of faith in Islam.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rahma, mercy, named twice in a row. Your line was mercy twice before anything else. Two weeks today. Day fourteen.

A shopkeeper's ledger has two columns: what came in, and what went out. Most of a life never makes it into a ledger. Dishes washed that weren't yours. An angry text deleted before it was sent. A night spent sitting up with someone, never mentioned again. Nobody writes the quiet things down. And on the other side, the things nobody caught. Today's verse says both columns are kept. Dropped into a prayer about mercy, that can sound like a warning. Listen to where it sits.
screen: `A LEDGER WITH TWO COLUMNS.` → `THE GOOD NOBODY WROTE DOWN.` → `BOTH COLUMNS ARE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Verse four: “Owner of the Day of Judgment.” In Arabic, maliki yawmi d-din. Today's word is the day itself: yawm ad-din. Yawm is day. And din, translated judgment, is also the everyday Arabic word for religion, a way of life. At its root it carries the sense of a debt coming due, an account settled. So this is the day when every account is squared: both columns, the unseen good and the unfinished wrong. Now, where it sits. Praise, then mercy, then mercy again, and only then the Day. The one just named merciful, twice, is the one who holds the account. Some readers take that order as the point: the reckoning isn't in the hands of a stranger, or an enemy, or a machine. It's held by mercy. And in that reading, nothing quiet is lost: the dishes, the unsent message, the night beside someone. In the conversation from day two, God answers this verse too: My servant has glorified Me. Some tellings add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me. Read that way, the verse isn't dread. It's handing the account over.
screen: `YAWM AD-DIN — THE DAY OF THE ACCOUNT.` · `DIN — A DEBT COMING DUE.` · `HELD BY THE ONE NAMED MERCIFUL.` · `HANDING THE ACCOUNT OVER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one good thing you did that nobody noticed. Let it be small. Hold it, and let it be enough that it happened. Then one thing you'd like to settle well: an apology, a debt, a promise. Don't solve it. Just set it down in front of you, honestly.
Yawm ad-din. The Day of Judgment, held by the one just named merciful. Fourteenth word. Salaam, the five pillars, salat, alhamdulillah, Rabb, rahma, yawm ad-din: that's week two.
Your line: the account is in kind hands. Nothing quiet is lost. Two weeks, done.

screen: `DAY 14 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "THEE (ALONE) WE WORSHIP; THEE (ALONE) WE ASK FOR HELP."`

pairs: judgment, religion, a debt coming due
the unseen good, the unfinished wrong

myth: this verse comes before any mention of mercy
it comes after mercy is named twice: in verse one and verse three.
din can also mean religion, a way of life
the same word: and at its root, a debt coming due.
in the conversation hadith, God answers this verse with a threat
My servant has glorified Me; some tellings add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me.

fork.setup: in the conversation hadith, someone praying says: Owner of the Day of Judgment. how does God answer?
fork.reveal: My servant has glorified Me; some tellings add: My servant has entrusted his affairs to Me. not a threat, a handing-over.

original.note: Arabic: the Day of Judgment. din also means religion, a way of life, and carries the sense of a debt coming due.

trapdoor: what you thought: the scary verse in the middle.
what it means: a day when every account is settled, held by the one named merciful twice before it.
what a scholar hears: two accepted readings, maaliki (owner) and maliki (king); din from a root of debt and requital; and the verse is the hinge between praise (verses 2–3) and address (verse 5).

sources.ref: Qur'an 1:4
